utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We have submitted a brief pleading to the Court today to summarise our position regarding late disclosure of these transcripts. I had the opportunity yesterday to go back and research the record and it appears to be the case that the Prosecution's had these transcripts for at least six months and has actually used them in the cross-examination of our witnesses. In addition, we've previously told the Trial Chamber that we had attempted to acquire copies of these transcripts that had already been provided to the Prosecution. We've made requests to the office of the president in June of last year and those requests were declined. We were told instead to try to get these documents from the Prosecution itself. We made a request in August and that was ignored. And so that's the -- that's the position with respect to lateness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you speaking about all the transcripts when you say the Prosecution had them for at least six months?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: I can't, in all good conscience represent to the Trial Chamber that the Prosecution's had them all. I don't know which ones we've had and which ones we've not had. But two of the transcripts, actually three of the transcripts that the Prosecution are seeking to have admitted, as we have stated in our papers, clearly form the basis of cross-examination last June and last July of our witnesses DA and DK and that's just inescapable. I do recall an exchange with the -- between the Presiding Judge and the Prosecution when, during the cross-examination of Witness DA, and recited on page three, I think, of our pages, page two, -- yes, page two, where the Prosecution was actually reading from one of these transcripts during the cross-examination of one of our witnesses and the Presiding Judge said, "What are you reading from?" And the Prosecution said, "Well, I can't tell you but I might tell you ex parte." We would suggest to the Court that that revealing exchange speaks volumes with respect to the claim that these are new documents. And that was an exchange that occurred on the record on June 9th, 2000, Your Honours. But turn to go where we left off yesterday which I think was number 8, transcript number 8 on our list, September 15th, 1993. Sorry -- yes, September 15, 1993, this appears to be cumulative and irrelevant and there are all sorts of hearsay and opinions uttered by the declarants not really going to any of the central issues in this case and certainly not going to the central issue of the culpability velle non of Mr. Kordic. With respect to the ninth transcript, October 22nd, 1993, same thing. Same arguments and I won't repeat them Your Honours except to say that I think Rule 89(D) considerations most definitely come into play here at this late stage of the game given the contentions exchanged between the participants in that meeting. With respect to number 10, the November 5th, 1993 transcript of a meeting that occurred at the Vila Dalmacija in Split, we have no record of having that transcript disclosed to us. I believe we cannot determine whether the entire Croatian version has been disclosed to us but which did not receive any English translation at least that was the case as of the date that our pleading was filed, November 15th. And if you'll permit me, I'll just inquire whether we've actually received a copy of the English translation between November 15th and today.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Regrettably, we simply cannot determine from the documents that have been provided to us whether an English translation has been disclosed. I don't recall one, but our records don't disclose the disclosure of one. With respect to number 11, transcript dated November the 6th, 1993, this transcript has been disclosed but it doesn't mention Kordic in any way, and we would simply suggest to the Court that it is of extremely peripheral relevance, if at all. It certainly doesn't go to the question of Mr. Kordic's criminal culpability or lack thereof. Exhibit number 12 -- sorry, entry number 12, the transcript dated November the 23rd, 1993. In addition to the objections that are stated in our pleadings, it seems to be almost completely irrelevant to the core issues in this case as the Court has previously articulated the test to be. And the same is true of the November the 28th, 1993 transcript, entry number 13 on our summary. Going over to entry number 22 on our summary, the February 13th, 1994 transcript. We have only had small excerpts of this translation produced -- English translation produced to us. As I said yesterday, I have not had the time to go over this full document with my Croatian-speaking colleagues, but it does appear to be of extremely dubious relevance based upon the representations made on pages 19 and 20 of Exhibit Z2833. And also -- actually, this is the transcript that was used during the cross-examination of Witness DA back in June of this year, June the 6th, I think. So this one, clearly, is not new. Item number 23 on our summary is March the 22nd, 1994. We don't have a copy of this transcript in Croatian or in English. So I'm not in a position to address whether it's in any way relevant to the case. And finally - I think it's finally - entry number 25, June the 11th, 1994. It's difficult for me to conceive what possible relevance this transcript has. It's beyond the period covered by the amended indictment. It doesn't relate in any way whatsoever to criminal culpability or the core issues in the case. And we've only received a partial translation in English of this document, so I don't know what the entire document deals with. But according to the summary, we would suggest to the Court that you can read the summary and exclude it on the basis of that. It's just tangential, cumulative, and it doesn't go to the central issues in this case. Let me just conclude the argument with this observation,

utterances.speaker: MR. PRESIDENT
utterances.text: The Court's previously told the Prosecution on several occasions that it really should adopt a robust attitude towards this Prosecution. This isn't simply an exercise of dumping every conceivable piece of paper that deals with a subject or mentions a subject into the record. It has got to have some relevance, especially at this stage to the game, to the central issues in the case. And I end where I started out. It appears that we seem to have lost the view of the wood for the trees, and we really need to get down to brass tacks here with documents that really relate to the central issues rather than cluttering the record with a vast array of peripheral and irrelevant material which is completely cumulative to the points that have already been made over and over again. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'll hand something to the legal officer, please. Yes, Mr. Mikulicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. First, on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Cerkez, I entirely agree with my colleague Mr. Sayers as far as the analysis of the content of this transcript is concerned for which the Prosecution wants to introduce as evidence. I think that the key issue is what my colleague Mr. Sayers said, which is that we think that we have lost the wood -- the view of the wood for the trees. We are now discussing the content of these transcripts and trying to evaluate their relevance without having done previously something that I consider to be a precondition to discuss the content of these transcripts, and the precondition is to establish the authenticity of these transcripts. These are the documents which the Prosecution requests to be admitted into the evidence and thus the burden of proving authenticity of these documents rests with the Prosecution. What have they offered us? The Prosecution brought in two witnesses - one of them was an audio recorder and the other one was a typist - in order to prove that during the relevant time, in Tudjman's office there were meetings held which were recorded and, thereafter, transcribed into the form of a transcript. Nobody disputes this fact. What we do contest, however, is whether the documents that have been offered to us, whether they are authentic and whether they really represent the conversations that took place in Tudjman's office, and the Prosecution has not offered any evidence to support this. There are no tapes that could help us verify the authenticity, to compare the transcript with the audio record. There are no videotapes that could serve to establish this very fact as well. There are no computer records, computer disk records. And finally, there is no testimony of those who were present at the meetings and who could verify the authenticity of these documents as to the contents. So our conclusion is that the authenticity of these transcripts has not been proven, and we further claim that they are not authentic. Now, this whole conversation reminds me of a situation in which somebody finds a hundred dollar bill on the street and then thinks about other things that could be bought with a hundred dollars and makes all kinds of plans, at the same time disregarding the fact that the hundred dollar bill is a forgery and cannot be used to purchase anything. So what we claim is the following: That these transcripts are simply pieces of paper with certain text on them, and the credibility, authenticity of these documents has not been proven by the Prosecution. As one of the arguments of the doubtful authenticity of these documents is further substantiated by the fact that after there were various write-ups in Croatian media, there was a proceeding initiated in Croatian parliament, there was a committee that was designed to verify the privatisation process of a large company, and these transcripts were offered as evidence in those proceedings. But for the very reasons that I have mentioned, the parliamentary committee refused to use these transcripts as valid evidence, especially since some of the participants of those meetings disputed the contents of these transcripts as they were shown.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Mikulicic, the fact that some other body refuses to accept the documents as authentic is not relevant to our proceedings. We have to deal here with the evidence in front of us, and apart from assertions by the Defence, there's no evidence or no material on which you can rely to suggest that they aren't authentic or perhaps you would point to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MIKULICIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I appreciate your comment, and with all due respect, I want to say that I did not bring out this example by the Croatian parliamentary committee as a precedent because this would be disrespectful to this Tribunal. However, I do wish to underline that it is not up to the Defence to prove that this transcript is not authentic or credible but is up to the Prosecution to prove that they are. So the Defence is claiming that they are not credible and to further this, we have offered further evidence. On the other hand, Prosecution is claiming that they are credible; however, they have not offered any evidence to support this and this is what we want to bring to your attention. I do not wish to trouble you any further, but I would like to state in my conclusion that these transcripts cannot pass your standards for admitting the documents because these transcripts are such that the Rule 89(D) needs to be applied to them since their probative value is questionable, at least to me. And on the other hand, their admission would cause significant detriment to the accused and this is why we think that Rule 89(D) needs to be applied in this case and these transcripts need to be excluded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Ms. Somers, as far as I am concerned, you need concentrate on these matters only, and those are the disclosure matters. The suggestion, first of all, that the material was not disclosed until -- at least some of it was not disclosed until after the 30th of October. The second point which is made is that the Prosecution have had the transcripts for six months and not disclosed them. And thirdly, the point that many of the pages are missing in the sense that selections have been made and the whole transcripts have not been disclosed. If you'd like to address us on those matters, you can. As far as the other matters are concerned, they have been fully addressed already.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, the other point is that they have been handed over in mainly B/C/S, as I understand it, and not in English.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. If I may request the Court's indulgence, I will address the points that the Court has asked for. I may ask for supplemental information from Mr. Scott simply because we've had a division of labour. I believe for just a few moments it may be necessary to ask for private session because there are will be some references made that will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, the -- referring to the point made by the Defence that on the documents that were turned over on the 13th of November which physically came in after the October 30th deadline, the Office of the Prosecutor only received those documents on the 13th of November. As I had indicated, Mr. Scott may best be able to tell you the difficulties in obtaining them, and that may end up with a quick return to closed session. However, as soon as we got them that very day, they were turned over in the B/C/S format, immediate translation was requested, and -- if they've been provided, then as soon as we get the translations they are immediately turned over. There is no delay on our part. However, the content of these documents, as I understand, was, in fact, made available to the Defence, so there is no prejudice. And this is how the process has worked consistently. As the Court probably understands, we are very much at the mercy of many factors that are well outside our control. Some are somewhat diplomatic and some are simply of persistence, bureaucratic. However, the requests were made upon identification and with repeated insistence on turning over, and ultimately they came, albeit not within the time frame that we had certainly hoped for. If there are no other issues other than the points there, if there is anything specific about the disclosure aspect that I may ask my colleague Mr. Scott to address, I would be grateful for the Court to let me know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. We'll accept what you say, Ms. Somers. There is nothing more to be added.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The other point is the question of selection of material and not all transcript being handed over.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. In terms of -- the entirety of the translation, is this what the Court is referring to?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is the submission that has been made by Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: This is this morning's. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It was made yesterday --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: -- according to my note. What he says is - let me just summarise what I have noted - that there are thousands of pages in the original. The Prosecution have selected parts of the transcript and the Defence have not had all the original in English. This is what I understand the submission to be.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In terms of the translation of selected parts, that was a decision that was made based on the limitation of resources within the translation services. It is true that there are indeed thousands of pages. The B/C/S originals have at all times -- I should say that they've been turned over. We had to make a reasonable selection of those points which go to either core arguments or form the basis for which we are seeking the admission. The process was not unique I think to this exercise. I believe earlier on in some -- early in this proceeding, with other witnesses, we had discussed with the Chamber and with counsels opposite the need for partial translation of relevant materials where it went on and on. We found under the circumstances, Your Honours, this was the only realistic way to do this. Indeed, if there are other portions of the transcript -- in other words, the entire B/C/S transcript certainly is available. If there are portions that are raised into question and that are specifically brought to our attention, we can, within the confines of whatever interpreter services or translation services can do, attempt to embellish, but it is, honestly, unrealistic given the literally thousands of pages. Sadly, this is beyond our ability. We thought this was the most reasonable approach. If the Court has some guidance for us or if the Court has some concern, I would very much appreciate being able to relay this to Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you for those explanations.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think there's anything which we need to ask you about, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: May I address the Court one second?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yesterday, and Mr. Tomljanovich has pointed out that there was a translation or there was a document that I believe we had indicated should have gone from the original document that the Court was looking at, and I think it probably bears a date on the very first one of 22nd of March. It is the ERN, which is the most critical of identifying marks, is -- are on the B/C/S it was R0157586 through 7651 and on the excerpted pages it is R0157605 through 7614. It is my belief that we may have had at all times incorrectly the date. It may be March 14th in the original B/C/S. It appears on the -- it appears as number 23 on the most current edition of this table. I'm sorry, on the earlier decision. And on the most current one it appears as number 22 and it is marked as Z1394.1. I just wanted to bring to the Court's attention and counsel opposite's attention that may be that we have simply mistranscribed the date on the original document, but it is before Your Honours for consideration as part of the admission. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll go on next to the Cerkez documents. While that's being done, Ms. Somers, can I raise something with the Prosecution. I still do not have from the Kordic documents the original of 1356.4. Now, it may well be that it's been handed in and may well be that it's somewhere in transmission, but I would like a copy of it by the break, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is going to deal with the Cerkez documents?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: It will be Mr. Lopez-Terres, and it may be beneficial --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Prosecution, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, you've, hopefully, sent in a list of documents that you particularly rely on, 28. We've got in front of us a nine-page schedule. I think probably from the two we can see what it is that you particularly want us to consider. Now that we have it in front of us, is there anything about any of these documents or about the documents generally about which you would like to address us?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you have said, Mr. President, we have gone through the list again. In that list you had more than 100 documents, 111 documents, to be precise, and we have reviewed this list very carefully using the criteria defined by the Chamber two days ago, and we would now have come up with a new list that counts 28 documents in total. Out of these 28 documents, you will note that item number 5, number Z660.2, this is a document that had also been listed in the list of miscellaneous documents, a list that we will talk about later on, I suppose. The comments, the observations about the document on the original schedule of 111 documents, well, these summaries, we stick to them. We believe that the 28 documents that make up the final list that we would wish you to admit in the evidence about the accused Cerkez or the brigade he was commanding, we believe that these documents are necessary to understand the case. They bring a new light to the case. They are not cumulative. And these documents made it possible to understand what was the framework in which Cerkez had a role to play as regards to certain facts. It gives some information about the structure of the brigade he was commanding. It was not the brigade that has absolutely nothing, the brigade made up of peasants, without any equipment, as has been said many times. So these documents shed new light and therefore we believe that we were perfectly justified that we are submitting these 28 documents for them to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Help us with the principle on which you were working. I know you were trying to follow our guidance but when you applied it to these documents, why did you particularly select these?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When we identified these specific documents we took account of several criteria. First, the fact -- the functions of the accused Cerkez in the municipality of Vitez and in the municipality of Novi Travnik where he was the deputy commander of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade. He was also the acting commander of that brigade in January and in February after the departure of the actual commander, Borivoje Malbasic. We have also selected documents that give additional information about the organisation of the Vitez Brigade, an organisation that was much more sophisticated than has been told to us by the Defence. This Brigade had an actual structure, had a commanding structure, had professional units. We have figures here about the brigade. I am referring you to 569.1. We see that right from the 22nd of March, you have 240 soldiers of the brigade that have been deployed. We have info here about where they have been deployed and as you can see, and contrary to what the Defence told us, this Brigade was not deployed mainly on the Serbian front. Only 60 soldiers have been sent to the Serbian front. You will also see in this document that 30 soldiers of this brigade are deployed in Busovaca. The Defence has always told us that Mr. Cerkez or his brigade had never had anything to do with Busovaca. Mr. Cerkez is charged in the indictment for facts that took place in the municipality of Busovaca as well. So this is the logic we have adopted for selecting this document, the direct participation of the accused in the establishment of a number of reports especially reports drawn up on the 16th of April, 1993, where it gives information about the progression of his forces in the various municipalities covered by the indictment. We spoke about Ahmici, Gacice, Donja Veceriska. These documents were either drawn up by the accused himself or representatives of his brigade, his officers were drawing up operational reports, combat reports, all these documents are very telling about the involvement of the brigade. We have also selected a number of documents that demonstrate that this was an offensive operation, an attack on the part of Vitez Brigade that was launched on the 16th of April. We have here documents of the -- of Colonel Blaskic where he asked for positions to be maintained on lines that -- on front lines that have been won over. So here, we have nothing to do with defence operations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me interrupt you. It may be helpful if you would point us to those documents you've referred to about the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are many reports dated the 16th of April that we have selected. We have selected them because they show that the brigade was involved and it shows its area of responsibility, and we have chosen these reports because some of them indicate the hour, the time of day when they were submitted because it's not always the case for other documents. And since a number of reports have been submitted on that particular day and it's a sequence, a chronological sequence of reports, we thought that it was important to have some idea about the time of day when the reports were produced. So it's important for some reports while you don't have the time of day, it's important to refer to the previous report and the next report to have some idea where a particular report is situated in the sequence. As for the reports for the 16th of April, I would refer you 663.4 in paragraph 2, it is stated that, "The command of Vitez Brigade has become an objective of the counter attack of the Bosnian forces." This is significant --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, is it 663 or 673.4?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 673.4, paragraph 2. In paragraph 2, the responsible officer of the Vitez Brigade admits that the command of the brigade has become a target. And that's very interesting because at the same time, Muslim civilians are detained in the HQ. So it's very interesting that these people are used as human shields to protect the command of the brigade and the use of human shields is part and parcel of the indictment, and we believe this document is an admission by the brigade of the use made of detainees as human shields. Another document of the 16th of April, 673.6, document Z673.6. In paragraph 4 of that document, Mr. Cerkez signs the document, is the signatory of the document, says that, "It can be concluded that the development of military operations has not gone according to plan." So here, they make specific reference to a plan and we believe that this is important and needs to be underlined. Following document Z673.7, report dated 16th of April, 10.00 in the morning. This report is very interesting because it is the confirmation by the accused, by Mario Cerkez. It's the confirmation that handwriting mentions notes that the Defence has mentioned very often, for example, the one we found on 692.2 where we are told that this is not authentic. Well, these type of handwritten notes are confirmed by the accused in this particular report where it uses information that -- where it had been handwritten on the back of the report requested by Colonel Blaskic. So as I said earlier, here we have nothing to do with defensive operation. We are told that the forces are moved towards Vrhovine and other places. We have been informed that a truce is being offered. And these are words that you can find almost word for word on Exhibit 692.2. And here the accused confirms the state of the military operations. I said earlier on that Colonel Blaskic uses a very offensive rhetoric language. It's very clear in Z673.9 document, 16th of April, in the morning. We are told that they need to fortify the positions, paragraph 5, maintain the combat readiness of the forces on the lines that have been won over. This is not a defensive type of rhetoric. This is part -- it's not the type of situation as described by the Defence. We also have from Colonel Blaskic another document dated 17th of April at 4.00 in the morning, Z693.1. In paragraph 7, Colonel Blaskic uses again the instructions given on the 16th of April in the morning, i.e., take over Donja Veceriska, take the fire station, Kruscica, set up blockades, et cetera. So we have exactly the same type of wording as in the order of the previous day. And in paragraph 8, once again, it is stated, "We have fulfilled 80 per cent of our objectives to date." So it's not the language used by somebody who is on the defensive faced with a major offensive from the other side, from the Bosnian army. So these were only a few indications that I wanted to give you, that I wanted to give the Chamber about the 16th of April. About another day, the 19th of April, Z726.3, Z726.3 seems to be particularly important especially in the last part, second page in the English version. A document dated 19th of April, it comes from the Vitez Brigade and it -- the 19th of April was the day of the bombing of Zenica that is disputed by the HVO. Here we can read, "If attacks intensify from Zenica, we propose the attack of the artillery, both from light and heavy artillery." On that day, the 19th of April, the state of mind of the HVO is very telling because that's the day when Zenica was shelled. We believe that this document is very important. We believe it is essential to establish the link between what happened on the 18th of April in Zenica around 1.00 p.m. or noon when the town was shelled, and the indirect admission by the operational officer of the Vitez Brigade of the state of mind of them on that day, the use of artillery to prevent the counter-offensive from Zenica. On 20th of April, same thing, 664.1 [sic], an officer of the Vitez Brigade, 1.30, once again, and using the same formula you heard about other villages, here we are at Gacice, again the municipality of Vitez. And the village of Gacice was done 70 per cent, and towards the end of the day it will probably be under the control. And you also have similar reports about other villages falling within the area of responsibility of the Vitez Brigade. So these are some of the illustrations covering particularly that period of time between the 16th and the 20th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. What was the number, Mr. Lopez-Terres, of the last one which -- last exhibit which you've said referred to Gacice?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Gacice, it is Z764.1 yes, this is a mistake it says "647." It is 764.1. During that period of time, which was the most active period in the Vitez area, it is also curious -- it is also interesting to record the order of Mario Cerkez on the 22nd of April. The brigade commander bids the -- there is the order concerning Z68 -- 781.1 and which is the order which forbids his subordinates to wear black shirts. And this is because they're trying to attribute the responsibility for the crimes which occurred in Vitez to the units which were wearing black uniforms, and these units apparently were not under the command of Mr. Cerkez. On the 22nd of April, Mr. Cerkez, while the fighting goes on, he forbids the men to wear black uniforms in order to indicate that there were only special units that wore those uniforms and in order to show that the -- trying to show that the brigade was not implicated, because there were several witnesses who spoke about men wearing black uniforms. Other categories of documents, Mr. President, Honourable Judges, we thought that it was important to show, by way of different examples, that the units of the Vitez Brigade worked in close cooperation and full coordination with special purpose units which were described as the units implicated in the crimes, specifically the regional police, the Vitezovi forces. These units, and it repeatedly turns out, worked under the control, under the authority of the accused Cerkez or his subordinates. An example, Mr. Cerkez, on the 26th of April, 1993, which is Z824.1, shows that Mr. Anto Bertovic, whom you saw here, who was one of the battalion commanders on the 26th of April, shows that there were units of the regional police and HOS which were at Krcevine and which were under the authority of the battalion commander of the Vitez Brigade, the subordination of authority in the area of responsibility of the brigade of the accused Cerkez. We also have other examples of the same kind and which are among the documents which we selected. There is Z1188.1, 1188.1, where it is intimated on behalf of Mr. Cerkez and his command that the units of the 3rd Battalion of the regional police are requesting from -- are requesting from the brigade -- requested by the brigade and the civilian police are attached to the battalion as a reinforcement. These units, therefore, worked again under the authority of the accused Cerkez. And this is an even more telling proof in the report of the fighting on Z1196.2, 1196.2, which is the report on the fighting, which is again a report made by one of the subordinates on behalf of the accused Cerkez and which says, "We wish to use the forces of several battalions with the assistance of some members of the Vitezovi force for -- and the military police and also some of the forces from Nova Bila." There were the already notorious forces in Nova Bila that were already mentioned, and those were the units under ill-famed Mr. Zuti. And Mr. Cerkez, as the commander of the brigade, therefore, had under his command in some of the operations which are mentioned in this document units which were from outside the brigade itself but were under his command. Another category of documents which we also selected concerns disciplinary matters, that is, how the brigade commander, the Vitez Brigade commander, how did he address disciplinary problems. And we have some documents to show that discipline was not really a concern in the brigade. There are some documents which show lack of organisation in -- and it happened several times during the period under consideration. These documents, to our mind, attest to the scarce concern of discipline in the brigade. You have already heard the testimonies which you heard, and the Defence tried to show that disciplinary measures were applied regularly against soldiers, but they do not seem that they were systematic in the Vitez Brigade. Quite the reverse; there seems to have existed a certain extent of disorder. The last documents, if I may and then I will conclude with what concerns the accused Cerkez -- I did not go through all the documents. Of course, once again I wish to repeat that we believe that all the documents that we selected following this latest analysis should be admitted by the Chamber, but I shall now mention two categories of documents which do go beyond the time frame concerning the accused Cerkez. Nevertheless, we believe they offer explanations and clarification of the whole case. That is a report which comes from SIS, this famous intelligence and security organisation. This is a report which is Z1316.8 [sic], 136.8 [sic] and this is the report of the 23rd of November, 1993. This report is about the situation in the different units in Central Bosnia. I should like to specify that in the original document, as you will see, has the letterhead of the HVO, that is, that SIS was a unit which operated within the HVO. It was not an autonomous unit, a unit which was outside the HVO. It made an integral part of the HVO, and that explains the letterhead in documents Z1315.8 and shows that the armed forces of the -- of Herceg-Bosna. It shows that there was a unit for intelligence and security. This report is interesting because in its final part, it makes a special reference and indicates a special relationship which existed between the accused Mr. Cerkez; Mr. Darko Kraljevic commander of Vitezovi; and Mr. Zeljko Andric, who is better known as Zuti and who also commanded a special purpose unit. And it notes that between the 18th and 23rd of October, Mr. Cerkez regularly visited Zuti or, rather, Mr. Andric, who had been wounded and who was recovering in Croatia in the house of Darko Kraljevic. So they were very close relations between the commanders of units. There are photographs and, therefore, it is easy to refute the allegation of the Defence according to which the accused had nothing to do with Mr. Kraljevic or with Zuti. And one can see that behind Mr. Cerkez there are other local public figures who are visiting Zuti. They were all visiting one another. They were on close terms. And there is Mr. Anto Valenta who visits him; Mr. Marijan Skopljak who also visits him, that is, head of the defence office in Vitez; Mr. Vlado Cosic, who is the assistant in the regional police. And the last document, the last document to which I want to draw your attention which is also beyond the time frame covered by the indictment insofar as the accused Cerkez is concerned but which reveals or confirms, if it is necessary to him once again, the link which existed between military and political authorities in Vitez, and this is Z1333.6 [sic], 1335.5, and which is a report of the second session which the HDZ party held in Vitez and which invited Mr. Cerkez, the brigade commander, to attend, who then explained to the party the military situation in the Lasva Valley, the situation of his brigade, and who also explains the how the relations between the military authorities and the political authorities or, rather, the municipal authority of the HDZ in Vitez, how these relations were always very close and friendly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kovacic, are you dealing with these documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will. [Interpretation] To begin with, just for the record, I do not accept the interpretations of documents as read by my learned friend. It seems to me that some of the interpretations, it seems that we've been watching some other film so far. And it seems to me, that is rather absurd when after all this evidence now at this point in the case, the Prosecution claims that Zuti, Vitezovi, and everybody was under Cerkez's command. I think it is an absurd claim. However, I prepared my evidence on the basis of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I don't think that claim is being made or if it is, then I have misunderstood it. I think the claim which is being made is there was a close connection between Zuti and your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It appears to me that it was at least twice mentioned that they were under the command, perhaps not Zuti but the regional ones and the Vitezovi. But I thought that our task today was, at least that is how I understood it, and I apologise, not to deliver our closing arguments or interpret conclusions that somebody might draw from these documents, but try to see the first place if -- whether the documents fit into the criteria that were laid down by you. Yes, perhaps one needs to add a word or two here and there for illustration and that is in this period that I should go through the document. The first document which was shown is 365.2. Now, my objections are as follows: To begin with, he was not on the index of the Prosecution's material of the 30th of October by which time they had to disclose these documents and these documents were disclosed only on the 18th of November which was after the deadline. Secondly, the document bears no archival stamp on his origin, and I wish to remind you that Witness Prelec said here before this Chamber that such documents without stamp mostly come from Samobor. And that is that if this document is a Zagreb document at all, then it must have arrived as early as May. So the Prosecutor could have disclosed it earlier. That is not a new material as you established in the first paragraph of your test. The document itself is repetitive and it shows that at some point, Cerkez figures as Malbasic's deputy when Malbasic is away, that he is not in the command and he, therefore, designates his deputy. But the Defence has already tendered a number of documents which it clearly indicated was never questionable all the positions of Cerkez for the whole period of the indictment. And we said it here, we saw documents and we heard live testimony. So if the Court believes that it is a genuine document, I will not object to it, but I think that it falls short of all the criteria which were set down. The next document is 490.1. We, again, think that it is repetitive on the basis of the same reasoning regarding Cerkez's positions. The Defence recognise all his positions even during the pre-trial brief and there is -- so that this document just unnecessarily encumbers the volume of all the evidence, and it is true that Cerkez does have this particular position which is here inferred and used to make all sorts of interpretations. Document 544.4. It, again, was not on the Prosecutor's index of the 30th of October. It was disclosed with a list of the 18th of November. It does not bear the archival stamp, and according to Witness Prelec, we can assume that it was obtained as early as May, according to an exhibit, I believe it was 321, it is repetitive. And again, because it refers to Cerkez's position, and we've heard quite a great deal about it. And as for the format of the document, it does not have the brigade stamp and we really do not know if it is a genuine document or not. The next document, 569.1, once again, was not on the Prosecution's index of the 30th of October. It was only disclosed on the 18th of November, does not have the archival stamp, that is why I believe this is not a document, and that they had it in May. It is largely repetitive. There is no new information in it or at least not any information which would be of relevance for the indictment, does not have the brigade stamp. Besides, it is cumulative and not particularly relevant. That is 99 per cent of the information in it can be gleaned from other documents and what, perhaps, cannot be gleaned are not relevant for the indictment. The next document is 660.2. Again, a document without the archival stamp. That is why we do not think it is new. It is largely repetitive. For instance, there are already a large number of exhibits to show that on the 15th of April, the HVO ordered a higher degree of preparedness in view of the proceeding events and about which there is a lot of evidence that is the abduction of officers of the Stjepan Tomasevic Brigade and Totic's, Zivko Totic's abduction. And we already saw documents in this regard warning of security. Now, all of a sudden, we have adduced the document of Sliskovic who is the security commander at that time and who is sending around a circular to raise the degree of alertness. I have nothing against those documents but it does not meet the criteria laid down because it is ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The microphone of the counsel is switched off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third document is 673.4. And if we agree that it was found -- even if we agree that it was found in Zagreb because it has the archival stamp, it is not a new document, obviously. And my colleague spoke -- referred to it at great length. He believes it's an important document. I don't see why. However, the document was introduced in Blaskic case, D273 and, therefore, the Prosecution must have had it if they worked with due diligence, even during the Blaskic case, and we could get it yet at the time of disclosure and this is a very serious -- very grave violation of the disclosure rule. I think the admission of this document should be denied because it is quite obvious that it should have been adduced then. The next document is 673.7. Once again, a questionable document as to its authenticity. It does not have the brigade stamp, the signature at the bottom which should be Cerkez's is quite different when a layman looks at it from his other signature. And if one looks at the format at least to the typewriter which is used, it looks different. It is one of the documents that we learned was in the possession of three intelligence services for at least six years and that is what makes it questionable. And in this sense, I do not think it fits into the criteria under Rule 89(D) because there were several Defence witnesses at the time when the Prosecution had this document. Perhaps the last witnesses who were here whom we could have asked about this document whom were perhaps aware of it, but we missed that chance and I think it would be highly prejudicial to the accused and in the case of that document, we really believe that Rule 89(D) ought to be applied. The next document is 673.9. It was also disclosed to the Defence on the 18th of November, that is after the deadline. The shortcomings are that it does not have a stamp, and it is a Blaskic document. And if I remember well, we did not see except for two or three of the huge number of Blaskic documents, we hardly saw any orders coming from his office which were not stamped. I think this is the second offered document of that kind, very, very limited number. Next document is 693.1. 693.1. This document also was not listed on the Prosecutor's index of October 30th, 2000. It lacks the stamp of the Zagreb archive which means that it was either found in Samobor or its origin is unknown. If it was found in Samobor, it means it is not a new document and, in addition to that, there is a great probability that it was introduced as Defence evidence in Blaskic which, unfortunately, we cannot verify because, as you know, we do not have an access to documents under seal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Pause there. The evidence should not be misstated. Mr. Prelec's evidence was that, of course, the Samobor documents did not have the archival stamp. Now, the fact that documents were disclosed at Samobor does not mean they can't be part of the documents which are disclosed today. The witness also said that not all documents from the archive had the archival stamp. Some were copied in the office and didn't have a stamp. So the evidence should not be misstated. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, naturally. But it does open new possibilities. What I'm trying to say is that there is a chance that these documents were in Samobor and we were confirmed this by Prelec at least as far as the Vitez Brigade documents, that most of them were in Samobor. Then we do know for a fact that Prosecution has these documents or at least we can conclude this, perhaps not with 100 per cent probability, but they've had these documents since May. And I was given these documents after the deadline that was established by the Trial Chamber, and some of them I was given on November 18th. My colleague noted that I skipped a document numbered 673.6. I have only one objection to this document. It does not bear a stamp. And 694.4, but this is the document that I was just going to speak about. So 694.4 was not listed on the Prosecution's index of October 30th. It also lacks the Zagreb archive stamp. It does not have the brigade stamp, is not signed, and differs in its form significantly. I would also like to bring to your attention a technical issue here, perhaps to be of assistance to the Chamber. You probably had an opportunity before to see documents of this nature, of this form, not only from the Viteska Brigade but others as well where in the background there is another text visible. At that time in Bosnia, they used quite an archaic, outdated system where they would use a paper for -- they would use a certain kind of paper in addition to carbon copies that could be used with carbon copies, and it was a very thin transparent kind of paper so that when the text was printed, you would obtain sort of two texts in addition to two documents unless one page was covered on the copier with another. We ran into these kind of documents several times, but I would just like to bring to your attention -- to point out that it is quite dangerous to use these kinds of documents. I myself did not dare use --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, when did you actually receive this document? You said it wasn't in the Prosecutor's index on the 30th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I lost track of the record. I cannot tell you with certainty. I think I was given this document either on November 18th or November 3rd, but do not quote me on this. It was not on the index of October 30th. We received it later, but I cannot tell you with certainty when. Next document, 724.4, I think is almost entirely irrelevant. It simply is a case of enlarging the file. This refers to the Blaskic indictment, obviously, with respect to his relationship with the UN, and I believe this to be completely irrelevant. Next document, 726.3, Z726.3. This document does not bear archival stamp. I refer here to Prelec testimony. And this indicates that the origin of this document is uncertain. We don't know if it comes from Samobor or elsewhere. This document was also not included in the October 30th list. Again I cannot tell you with certainty when it was delivered to us, but it was definitely after October 30th. As far as the document itself is concerned, it lacks the brigade stamp, has not been signed, and it is also cumulative because a large number of admitted evidence so far indicated that there were -- that there was combat in the areas that are mentioned in this document here. I don't see that this document brings in any additional information, any additional region which has not been mentioned previously. Another document, 764.1. The document itself bears an unknown signature which we were not able to identify, although we do know the signatures of officers on duty. It lacks the stamp of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, we're going to adjourn now. We would be assisted by the Prosecution at the end of this submission dealing with two matters. First of all, to ensure that these documents weren't exhibited in Blaskic as alleged. If you would check that, please, over the adjournment. And also deal with the allegation, suggestion, that documents weren't on the 30th of October list and were, therefore, delivered late. That's the other point. You can deal with that at the end. We'll adjourn now, rather shorter than usual because we want to finish in good time before 1.00, and, therefore, we'll take a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] And to conclude with document 764.1, the last thing we have to say about it is that we think that it is repetitive for practically all of its contents and, therefore, cumulative too. And since my learned friend especially referred to the event of the village in Gacice saying that it's been done 70 per cent, I should like to remind you that two other exhibits were adduced, that is, two reports of the Vitezovi unit, and these reports say that they were in Gacice. So if that is relevant, the brigade's report on the situation, then it could be interesting, but we know who did what in Gacice and we have evidence to that effect. So this is cumulative and it is not -- and does not have much probative value, that is, in that sense it is not particularly relevant. Let me just go back, if I may, to document 694.4. During the break, I found that this document was disclosed to the Defence on the 4th of September, that is after the deadline of the 30th of October -- no, excuse me, I was wrong, before. So this document was disclosed but it was not -- it did not figure in the index but it was disclosed. And just one more thing about the document that I was talking about previously, 764.1. I think that this document could also be viewed in the light of the criteria that you indicated under Rule 89(D) that is especially the facts here, what the -- regarding the time when the Prosecution seems to have had it in their possession. Had that document been disclosed in time, witnesses of the Defence could have testified about it because at that time, they were testifying before the Court and they could have told us something about that. As it is, the chance was missed and, again, this is yet another document which, for the past six years or so, was held by at least three intelligence services. The next document is 781.1, and that is the document which, again, merited special attention of the Prosecution. That is the order, Cerkez's order of the 22nd of April 1993 whereby he prohibits the wearing of black uniforms. All I have to say is that this was already discussed here, that it is therefore cumulative, and especially that in the introductory sentence, Cerkez refers to the order of his superior, that is the commander of the Operative Zone, refers to its number and the date and that order is in the files. Blaskic, as the highest-ranking commander, sends a circular letter to all brigade commands and forbids black or any other uniforms and Cerkez merely forwards that order as his subordinate. I do not see what one can conclude from that and what's the conspiracy that the Prosecution speaks about, that the commander is trying to introduce to make some order then he is accused of scheming and when he does not make order, then he is accused of not making any order. The next document is 781.1 [as interpreted]. Again, does not have the archival stamp. In its appearance, it is different from other documents coming out from the brigade command or rather we have not yet seen documents formatted as such. As to its contents, it's repetitive and the introduction shows that it refers to a circular letter. I also think that 89(D) is applicable here because it could have been disclosed earlier and shown to a witness. The next document is Z781.2 and here there is something which I wish to single out. This document disclosed to the Defence on the 2nd of October with another document referring to Rule 68. The second document was ERN-1001426 in the language of the original and in English it was L0017322. This document that is 781.2 does not have a stamp or a signature, and I think it comes under criteria envisaged by Rule 89(D). I should also like to suggest if the Chamber decides to admit it, then I should like to suggest that it be put together in one set under the mentioned ERN number because only those two documents together as one whole explain why is Cerkez issuing instruction because this is not an order. Why does he decide that some person should immediately be released. That is obvious only from that first document 01001426 which was disclosed to us. This document shows that Cerkez is writing a letter to his superior on the 22nd of April, 1993, and among other things, he says, "We deem it would be humane to release those persons and report to the International Red Cross and the ECMM in writing because they would perceive that as a humane gesture." And concludes that, "If you think that we should act differently, we shall conduct consultations to this effect." And after that, the next day, Cerkez decides that persons detained who are in the building of the command, that is in the cinema, that some individuals, several categories which are itemised here be released immediately. So that is only if we have both these documents do we get an answer to the question because it transpires from the second document which seems to be tendering itself. It shows that Cerkez ordered the release. The first document from which I just read a fragment, it appears that he is suggesting it to his superior because obviously it is not known who is responsible for those persons. So one can conclude that he received an answer in the meantime and that he is carrying out. But I think, and this is a very good example for Rule 89(D) that this is an important document even when these two documents are joined, it is an important document and the harm which it would cause would exceed the benefit because there are very many other documents testifying to the release of detainees. So that is as far as that document is concerned. The next document is 804.1, another document without the archival stamp so that its origin is questionable. And the Croatian document, that is, a copy of the original, is barely legible. One can read only a word here and a word there. I don't know on the basis of what the translation was done. And what is even more important, its contents are almost irrelevant or I could say completely irrelevant, or at any rate, it is not particularly relevant. The next document is 824.1. Again lacks the Zagreb stamp, the stamp of the Zagreb archive so that its origin is questionable. It was not on the Prosecution's index of the 30th of October, 2000, but I don't know when I got it. Its contents are irrelevant or at least not particularly relevant, and for the most part it is repetitive because it is a report notifying the Operative Zone about three locations in Vitez where some members of the regional police are HOS and some reconnaissance teams are positioned, and we have heard countless testimonies already that the Vitez Brigade held the front lines in principle and in special units intervened when those front lines would fall. And we have a statistical overview of the situation showing such-and-such units intervened here. The next document is 891.2. The Zagreb stamp is missing again and its origin is unknown. It is possible, I say it is possible, I cannot say that, that it could be deriving from the Blaskic case or, rather, was produced in the Blaskic case and the Prosecution had it at an earlier date and should have been disclosed earlier, but I cannot really affirm that because it could come from that part of Blaskic's transcripts which are not accessible to us. The next document is 978.1. Once again, there is no archival stamp; that is, we are not sure about its origin. Or if it comes from Samobor, then the Prosecution must have had it since May. I do not see anything relevant in that document or at least not particularly relevant, and it is largely repetitive because we have a great deal of evidence already about the events covered by this report. The next document is 1025.2. Again a document without a Zagreb stamp and same reasoning, and it is not of particular relevance or at least not a high degree of relevance. 1025.2 is the next document. Excuse me. No Zagreb stamp. The stamp of the Zagreb archive. It is not included in the Prosecution's index of the 30th of October, and it was disclosed to the Defence as late as November 18th, that is, after the deadline. Then 1085.5. Once again, there is no stamp from the Zagreb archive, so we're not sure about its origin. We do not have any other objections. The next one is Z1146.4. Once again, it lacks the stamp of the Zagreb archive. It is not on the Prosecution's list of the 30th of October, but in point of fact and regardless of these formal shortcomings, and we think that the criterion should be a formal one, as far as its contents are concerned, we do not object. We do not need it really because we believe it is repetitive. We do not think that that document is needed. The next document is 1188.1. My learned friend in the Prosecution attached great importance to this document, and I must say that I -- with all due respect, I don't see why. Namely, this report shows that some other units are active on the positions or synchronised with the brigade. That was the part pointed out, but we've heard a great deal of evidence about this. It is not something which is inadmissible. What it means is holding the front line and some operations. But in view of the criteria laid down by you, this again is a document without the archival stamp. So it either dates back to May or, rather, the Prosecution must have had it in May and it should have been disclosed much earlier. That is, it is not a new document, or it comes from some other source and then it is not really credible. It was disclosed to us on the 18th of November, 2000. And, in fact, to my mind its contents are irrelevant. We've seen such reports before, and there is nothing particularly new in any of its parts. Z1196.2. If my files are correct, this document was not on the list until the latest batch of disclosures when we were given the so-called clean material. It was not disclosed to us before that, that is, it was disclosed too late. It lacks the Zagreb stamp; that is, we know nothing about its origin. It is not on the index of the 30th of October, the index of the Prosecution, and in terms of its content, it seems to me that it is not relevant at all. If there is some relevance, then, again, it cannot be particularly high. The next document is 1228.2. It was disclosed to us only on the 18th of November. It does not have the archival stamp. It was not on the index, the Prosecution's index of the 30th of October, that is, as far as its form is concerned, but we do not object against its admission. But we think that it should have been disclosed to us in line with Rule 68, that is, at a much earlier date. But I requested a disclosure of documents under Rule 68. The Prosecution always claimed that they had disclosed it all to us. Now we see that that was not the case. The next document is 1315.8, and that is the first document which goes beyond the time frame of the indictment of Cerkez. It was not on the Prosecution's index of the 30th of October. It was disclosed to me on the 3rd of November. I believe it irrelevant for the Defence or the Prosecution or the incrimination of Cerkez. It is not signed. It does not have the seal of the author. It does not allow to draw any conclusions. My learned friend dwelt on it. In particular, I do not waste your time, and all I want to say is even if this is correct that among other public figures, Cerkez also went to pay a visit to Zuti who had been wounded, I really do not see any legal relevance. And it sounds to me not only the guilt by association but again, you frequent the same pub as the other two, and those two are thieves so you are a thief too. Except, of course, that the accuracy of that information is absolutely impossible to check not to mention the photographs. Not only the photographs, the quality of these photographs are such that one wouldn't be able to recognise one's own brother let alone somebody else. And to conclude, even if he did visit Zuti while he was on the sick leave, I see nothing bad about that. The last document is 1335.5. My learned friend attached certain importance to this document. Let me remind you that it's a document in which Cerkez is present as a guest of a meeting at a meeting of the municipal branch of the HDZ in Vitez on the 19th of December, 1993. That is far out of the time frame of the indictment. And the agenda of that meeting shows that the first item was the security. So the party, as I read it, wishes to make an assessment of the security situation in their place. They invited Mr. Cerkez. Mr. Cerkez, as a guest of the meeting, explained the situation in the Lasva Valley with the special reference to the territory of the Vitez Brigade. And two more sentences, nothing bad in them, saying that military authorities enjoyed full support of the HVO government in Vitez and that this cooperation was to the mutual satisfaction. He thanked the gentlemen at the forward office in Split, pointed out the need to mobilise our men and so on and so forth. And my learned friend says that this then gave rise to a lively discussion. If this is supposed to prove that the Cerkez were working with the -- for the HDZ, which seems important, then this document helps the Defence because this document clearly says that he was a guest at that meeting and we see that from its intervention and for the purpose which he was invited to the meeting. Needless to say, this document, like many others, are computer printouts without signature and, therefore, I do not think that it is particularly credible. And the long and short of it, I think it is irrelevant in Cerkez's case because he is being charged with what he did or did not do until the 30th of September, 1993 and this is after that. And to conclude, the first thing I want to say is that of the 28 documents selected by the Prosecution, 18 do not have the stamp of the Zagreb archive. Bearing in mind the testimony of Witness Prelec and the record on the handing over of documents which was adduced -- which was tendered in evidence with that testimony showing that the majority of documents for the Vitez Brigade were handed over to the Prosecution as early as May, I believe it shows that, for technical reasons, the Prosecution kept those documents in their possession and did not disclose them to the Defence. I also wish to remind you of the 16th of April when Cerkez was to testify, he received 40-centimetres high pile of documents. And we also discussed the document 692.2 and Prelec testified about this. Now, the Prosecution dropped it from their list, from this shorter list, and I should like to hear it from them whether they still want this document in and not to have to go back to that again. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Our time is short. Mr. Sayers, is there anything you want to say about these documents which we haven't heard already?

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Just one document, Your Honour. Z1335.5, November -- sorry December 19, 1993. Just want to underscore the point made by my colleague to the effect that this is just a computer printout. It's not signed by anybody. It doesn't have any official stamp. It's not on letterhead. And, as Mr. Prelec told us just a couple of days ago, there's no way to tell whether this was a draft document or a real document and there's no proof been adduced by the Prosecution as to where this was found within the archives and that's the only contextual help cited by Mr. Prelec, I think I am quoting him accurately. He said that you could only determine whether it was a real document from knowing exactly where it came from in the context of the archive and we don't have that proof here. But that's the only document that I wish to talk about specifically, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, if you could just deal with those matters we asked you to deal with. First of all, there were two alleged Blaskic exhibits. Is that right or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we have checked our records and only one document out of the documents produced was amongst a series of documents used in the Blaskic case. It's Exhibit 673.4, and there was a document used by the Defence in the Blaskic case that bore the number D273. In relation to that document, it's a document dated 16th of April. It's about the shelling of Vitez, especially the centre of the town where you had the general headquarters of the Vitez Brigade. This document bears the stamp of the archives, and I would like to mention that this -- it was not the case for the Blaskic document but I don't think that's the most important thing. At the beginning of my submissions, I said that as for the day of the 16th of April, we thought that it was important to show the judges that there was a sequence of reports, of orders that had been delivered during the morning of the 16th of April. And this particular document is the first in the series of documents, because this document was delivered at 9.00 in the morning on the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: But Mr. Lopez-Terres, if it was used in Blaskic, how can you say it's a new document?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not a new document in terms of information of the content of the document itself, but we deem that the documents bearing the Zagreb stamp could be used. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.text: [Interpretation] I indicated to the Chamber that there were two documents that you have on this list that had already been admitted. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In order to save time, Your Honours, we concur in what our colleague has just stated. And if I may, Mr. President, I want to point out just one more matter. utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know if the Chamber's brought with it its copies of the English translation of the diary today or not. I ask that it did equip itself with it, but that was a couple of days ago now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have here English and the Croatian. It seems to be 200-odd pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Dated the 11th of January or does it relate from the 16th of April to the 15th of May. I haven't looked at it in any detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's a document of very considerable value to the Chamber. It's a document which, on inspection of the original, the Chamber may readily conclude is simply not capable of being a concoction both by it's very form, and by its content and the context into which it can be placed. With the usher's assistance and to save time if I can just lay one page on the ELMO straight away, a page Mr. Sayers referred to earlier, an anomalous entry that in the English translation, you can find at page 23, but the way it's reflected at page 23 doesn't necessarily do justice to the original because what one can see on page 23 is simply the reference. But what one can see on the original is that those words about war diary from the 15th of April have been written over, for whatever reason, other entries that are all part of the January record of this diary. So that for whatever reason, and I assume it's written over as opposed to a copying error, somebody's done that and it's done that on that page. But that's the only odd feature. Now, if I could invite the Chamber, in order to assess the potential value and, again, the clear integrity of this document as a document, if I could invite the Chamber to come back to page 11 in the English and if the usher -- I've got some of these marked so that I may be able to display them without taking time. The Court will see, for example, an interesting entry towards the foot of the page for the 20th of January reflecting that Kostroman, it was, who was disarmed at the barricade which, of course, was not originally in line with the evidence that we were calling on this topic, although it may well become clear that that may well be right rather than it being Kordic or some combination of those that that, I think, can be found -- I just place that original straight away on the ELMO. If the -- you can see the references to Kostroman there, I think. Then we can -- if Your Honour turns over, for example, to page 12, I won't trouble the usher with this one for the time being, you can see in the middle of the page the explosive device at the bank. If the Court goes over then, I hope I'm not going too fast to page 617, we are now on the 24th of January, the second checkpoint incident and again one sees at the foot of the page, "1515. Shooting. One of our men killed," and 1545, confirmation that it was one man killed. The Court will have some recollection of the issues there between one and two men. If one turns on then to page 22 for the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Not too quickly for the interpreters or, indeed, me.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Where were you on the 24th of January?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I was on the 24th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Page 16 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Page 17 in English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it's "1515 hours. One of our men was killed."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Of course that -- just pausing there for a moment, we haven't got long, but to be entitled to rely on that, you would no doubt argue in rebuttal of the various points that have been raised.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Of course, yes. If we move on to another and extremely significant entry at page 22, for the 29th of January, the Court having in mind the tape-recording, the audio tape-recording of Kordic giving artillery instructions, the exhibit that is the subject of application in the Kordic papers from the man Batinic, who is referred to in the tape, the artillery officer, complaining about Kordic giving artillery instructions. Different degrees of detail being entered. Yes, I'll just put that one, I'm afraid I've marked that one slightly on the right-hand side, that one there. If we put this on the ELMO. You can see towards the bottom of the page where I've got a little red mark on the right the two references to Kordic. If we go to -- I'm going to pass over a lot of other entries for speed, but if we go to the -- if we go to page 39 for the 25th of February, there's a small entry there which will become of significance next week, in the course of next week's evidence, where there's a reference to the flag on the factory being taken down towards the end of February. There's going to be significant evidence in relation to that. I shan't say more about it, but significant evidence in relation to that next week. Then, if I can take you to the central issues at page 68. And at page 68, we are in the 15th of April. And as Your Honour will see, at the foot of the page, there is a reference to a meeting held at 1730 hours with the composition of the meeting set out. The Chamber will --

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hate to interrupt but in the document that's been given to us, page 68 has been missing. It goes from 67 to 69.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Can we have a copy of 68, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I lay mine on the ELMO? I remember that this was faxed to them on Saturday, and I also remember that there were difficulties with the Hunton & Williams fax machine, and it was a matter of discussion. Incidentally, that meeting - if the usher could be so good - is to be found on, I think, this page here. The entry on our page 68 actually crosses two pages, but you can see at the top of this page the -- yes. You can see part of the entry that I've just read out. And the Court will recall, I'm grateful for being reminded, the problems of late translation on receipt of this document from the Zagreb materials were eased by the fact that the translation we're working on was provided by the institution but initially to Defence in another case pending on appeal. If Your Honour then goes on to the 16th of April itself --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We could see there are references on the 16th to Mr. Kordic asking for information and ringing in regularly. That's no doubt the way you would put it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's absolutely right. And I must not understate the significance in order, as it were, to take advantage, after the event, of something I haven't drawn to your attention. Apart from the regular and I can't remember now how contacts it is between Kordic and Blaskic, there is, at Your Honours' page 94, and at two minutes past six, a critical entry or a very interesting entry, putting it at its mildest, about Kordic, the Colonel, and Pasko. And on page 87, at 1508, there is a reference to a report with its number, 12513. That is the document that's already been produced from Cerkez saying that the villages have been 70 per cent done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you the number of it, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, I haven't. It's my mistake. I've not put that down. We'll find that immediately, if we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.
