utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Puticevo. Just remind us where that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's just up the road from Vitez, in the direction of Donja Veceriska. I ought, of course, to draw your attention that at page 207, the last page of the document, and reflecting no doubt it may be his use of this document in preparation of his own case, but, nevertheless, Blaskic certifies that there are two pages probably been torn out deliberately because the time doesn't match noticed -- beg your pardon. He said noticed in June 1993. So not in relation to his case but be that as it may. The page numbers can be seen on the original. They're very difficult to find. They can be seen. And this document, like one other document which I do want to have a reference to later on very briefly, is a double-page document in the original. If Your Honour looks at what I'm holding up, it's a document that is constructed with open pages like that. It's a double-page document like that. And the numbers can just be seen sufficiently to trace down the missing pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It appears to have the archive stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's got the archive stamp on every page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So that particular argument is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Because the argument really is: At this stage of the trial should this document be admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, in our respectful submission, it is effectively a record of the activities, of the business. In business record terms, it would qualify. It's entered by a number of different people. Let it be said at once it doesn't go all one way because insofar as it contains passages alleging concern about Muslim aggression ahead of events, I can't argue that that's going to have been written down with any calculated or calculated plan. It's a document that's likely to be a reasonably accurate reflection of what was being done and said in the Hotel Vitez at the time. And you've seen again how the Kostroman point may well be a point that on that particular detail will rebound to the Defence advantage, although, as I've already said, our evidence, in they event, would probably be drifting towards that ultimate conclusion. I don't know if I can help further on the diary at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point in the case, after Mr. Kordic has closed his case, to have a document like this suddenly pop up containing these allegations against him, we would respectfully submit fundamentally implicate the considerations that lie at the heart of Rule 89(D). How in the world do we even know who actually wrote this book? Apparently somebody's been at it, as the Prosecution specifically noted. In the page 207 of the English translation anyway, apparently Colonel Blaskic has been at it and taken pieces out. Now, if he has taken pieces out, that leaves open the possibility that maybe he's put pieces in. And let me just suggest this to the Court: This is a document that covers January 11th, purportedly to May the 19th of 1993. Why does it start on January the 11th and why does it end on May the 19th. Where are the diaries before this? Where are the diaries after this? If this is real. Presumably these would have been disclosed along with the other documents in the Croatian State Archive. Why just those dates? A few other things for the Court to consider. In the Croatian original, Mr. President, there are 96 pages in handwriting written by who knows whom. I certainly don't. Now, Mr. Nice says, "Well, this is clearly from the Operative Zone." Well, how does the Court know that other than what Mr. Nice actually says? We would respectfully submit that it doesn't. The Prosecution hasn't produced a single authenticating witness to talk about this document. And they've had if for quite a time, and we suspect that they have, why wasn't this document put to the numerous people from the military organisations in the Viteska Brigade who have testified for months in this case? But think of this. Here just my observations, and I have only been through this document very briefly, Mr. President. The Court will recall that there was an outbreak of fighting in Busovaca on January the 25th. Now, this diary has three-quarters of one page devoted to that particular event, one of the most significant events in this trial according to the Prosecution. On April the 13th, there are three pages of entries. On April the 14th there's a half a page. On April the 15th, I believe, although I don't have that page with me and I want to say that Mr. Nice is correct, apparently his office did fax the April the 15th entry over to us last Saturday, I just didn't put it in the book here and I apologise for that, but apparently there's one page. April the 16th, 28 pages. Minute by minute. Now, who wrote those entries? Who recorded what was being reported about conversations that had apparently occurred over the telephone, hearsay several times removed? How do we know that those entries were, in fact, written contemporaneously, as the Prosecution contends, or not recreated after the event by someone, perhaps Colonel Blaskic, when he apparently reviewed this document at his leisure and removed pages from it? How do we know that? We don't. We're left in the realm of speculation and guess work and conjecture and there's no way to get us out of it, unfortunately, and that's really the heart of the matter under Rule 89(D). As Mr. Nice says, several of the entries in here contain recitations of what Mr. Kordic supposedly said or what Mr. Kordic supposedly ordered. Well, there's no indication that the recorder of events actually participated in those telephone conversations. So at a very minimum they'd have to be hearsay and second time removed even if they are contemporaneous entries and, respectfully, there's simply no way to verify that they are. What is true of April 16th is also true, I believe, of several of the subsequent days like April 17th, for example. I haven't counted up the number of pages, but they are not significantly less substantial than the April 16th entry. So if we are to believe this document of the 180 days that it supposedly encompasses, 30 per cent of it is devoted to one day. Now, to say that that strains credulity would understate the matter to some degree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be said, of course, but it may be said, and we would have to consider, whether those days which are the subject of most entries were the days that are subject of the most action, for instance, the 16th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Mr. President I take your point precisely. Then consider then the three quarters of the page that is devoted to the extremely significant outbreak of fighting in Busovaca that resulted in the loss of a significant the amount of territory, a significant amount on January 25th through or until January 30th when the cease-fire agreement was signed. 2.200 Croats kicked out of their homes between Kacuni and Bilalovac. Ten Croats massacred at Dusina. Not so much as an entry. No reference to that in this document, Mr. President. Why not? I mean this was one of the more significant events for Croats in the first half of 1993. This was the first massacre in the Lasva Valley. And I don't see any reference to it in this document. But you've got three quarters of a page devoted to the single-most significant outbreak of fighting before April 16th, and I absolutely take Your Honour's point. It's entirely possible that April 16th was singled out for particular attention because the most significant events occurred then. It is entirely possible. Yes, indeed, that is a possibility. But we need to take this document out of the realm of possibility, especially after we've closed our case, and inject it into the realm of certainty through authentication, through knowledgeable witnesses who participated in the drafting of this document and who can bring some personal knowledge rather than just bold argument from the Prosecution as to what these entries must necessarily mean to Mr. Kordic's significant and incurrable prejudice, we would submit. I think that pretty much covers the territory I'm interested in covering. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I do not think one should go into detail and analyse it in depth. We fully go along with what Mr. Sayers said. This document simply does not look convincing. We, in particular, agree that it should be viewed in the light of Rule 89(D) because the Defence would no doubt find itself in the predicament after the completion of both the Prosecution case and the Defence case. However, as for the value of the document as such, I'd like to remind you of one element. Alongside all that my colleague has said, the vital question is: When did this document come into being if it did? Not only because we heard Blaskic, himself, say that some pages had been torn out and there are some rumours that some may have been added, but the question is: When was it all written? I do not wish to waste your time by analysing various facts, but there are a number of contradictions here which seem to point in that direction. But since we have this document on the table before us today, I do not think there is any reason to use it unless we have a witness, as we did in a conventional manner with a number of other documents. A witness may know something about an event, and that can be source for our information. We can learn something from a document, and then we can ask the witness about this. But this document cannot become evidence, cannot become an exhibit until the Prosecution has proven its credibility, it's authenticity at a much higher level. And that should also include a live witness who would confirm the manner of writing this document at the time when it was written. Just a minor correction, I believe it was just a slip of the tongue, but perhaps it was deliberate. I do not remember it from the diary, but my colleague Nice mentioned a place called Puticevo and linked it to Donja Veceriska. They simply have nothing to do. Puticevo is far from us in Travnik. It has nothing to do with the municipality of Vitez, and I didn't get it whether you found it in the diary or whether it was the conclusion of my colleague, but they have absolutely nothing to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know I've already taken up my time, but could I make two very brief points? The first is during the cross-examination of Sir Martin Garett on February 1st of 2000, I showed Sir Martin a document and the question was put at me: "Are these documents which the witness is likely to have seen?" And I said, "I don't know without asking him now, Your Honour." And the instruction I was given was, "No, but these are matters which you must prove in some other way. It's no good just asking the witness when he has no recollection putting a whole lot of documents ..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you slow down, Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: My apologies to the interpreters. "... putting a whole lot of documents to him which he can't have seen. Let's move on. You can deal with this in your own case." And we surely would have dealt with this document in our own case if we had had it. And there's no excuse, five years after the confirmation of the original indictment and, might I say, Your Honour, after the entire trial in the Blaskic case, this is -- the Prosecution is a unitary institution. We don't re-invent or visit facts for the first time in this case. There are all of the other cases which the Prosecution has tried involving the facts in the Lasva Valley and yet, for the first time, we appear to be confronting this document. But the final point I wanted to make was we have had one witness talk about this document and only one witness, and that was Mr. Prelec on November 20th. And I'm looking at the -- page 27.266 and the one page that was the subject of questioning of Mr. Prelec, obviously was the one page which was of such concern to the Prosecution. I asked Mr. Prelec, how it came that the April 15th entry had been written over other entries in January of that purported document. "Q How is it that that entry is it right in the middle of a page dealing with events in January, do you know? A I have no idea." So I said, "Q Have you made any inquiries along those lines? A No. And frankly, I wouldn't know where to start. It appears to have been written over by someone else." And then this question, "Q And you don't know who wrote over it something else or when, do you? A No, that's correct." So the one page which has been examined from this document has a fundamental inconsistency on it which even the Prosecution's own witnesses can't explain, and under those circumstances, there's simply got to be a reliability component, Your Honour. Even if this were during the Prosecution's case in chief, and we would suggest that to the Court very earnestly that that suggests unreliability as does the fact that someone's been at this document, presumably Colonel Blaskic, for whatever reasons which I think we can all guess. But the point is at this late stage of the case, Rule 89(D) must come into play and if ever there were a case for the application of that rule, it's in this instance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I just make about four points?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Could you help us with this? Is there an original of this document anywhere available.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's still in the archive, I understand. We have the, of course, photocopy of the original. That's probably as good as we'll be able to do. If the Chamber wants the original itself, it conveys that to the archive, it may be that would have some effect of releasing it to us and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you tell us how the -- your office did get this copy from the archives?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Got it from the archive in the same way as it got the other documents as I understand it and it was brought up in photocopy form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Who copied that?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I would need I think to speak to Mr. Prelec about that, but I think that the copying was done for them not by them. So it was copied in the archive and handed over according to procedures, but I may need to check that and I'll do so. But the document would have been seen first of all by either Mr. Prelec or by one of the other people there and identify as a document that was wanted, and then it would have been copied and handed over. So that there's an ability to match what's been seen originally with what's provided.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: And to try to clarify what Mr. Sayers, his own doubts about the dates, he said this is one diary starting I think on January to such date. Are there other diaries in the archives other than this one?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There may be. That's another matter that I want to check because I was stimulated to think that, but I don't want to give you an answer until I have checked. So I'll check that and I'll try to get Mr. Prelec down here straight away. Can I make the following, I think, four or five points very briefly? No conceivable purpose to forge this document can really be established. It's suggested that Blaskic may have interfered with, but if one looks at the document as a whole for its manifest form and composition by different people, inconceivable that it could have been forged. It's a fantasy to think it could be. There comes a stage when, indeed, Mr. Prelec said in relation to a slightly a different topic, namely the overall archive, it is not a matter of expertise. It's a matter of common sense that it's beyond construction. Second, the document title is worth just having in mind. We've all been, perhaps, drawn by the words, "War diary", but what it's actually said to be is a book of observations of the officer on duty and that, of course, may very well explain why not only do you have different hands but you have a different degree of detail recorded not to account for the difference between the 16th and other days, but you may have a different degree of detail made by different reporting officers as reflected in the document generally. It was a document that came to us very late -- so sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BENNOUNA
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, can you help us? You said that this is different writing because it was written by the officer on duty. What was the role of Colonel Blaskic in regard of this diary when he signed at the end? What is his role exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I imagine as supervising officer, but it wasn't he who recorded things. And, of course, one of the explanations that one can offer as to why certain things are not on here is because the officer on duty will record and see and hear some things but not everything. And it's probably only what is recorded at base in his presence that gets recorded here. Consistent, of course, with a wide range of matters being recorded on the night of the 15th, 16th, and 17th when, on the evidence, things were being controlled from Hotel Vitez. Different considerations may well arise and did arise, of course, when either Blaskic was elsewhere in Kiseljak unable to get back to Vitez or out in the field. So that this is what the officer on duty at base is in a position to record and, according to his own habits or practices, did record. The reason that the document wasn't put to other witnesses because it wasn't available to us. Now, next week's witness may be able to help with it. I have to tell the Chamber, we're still in open session -- perhaps we can go into private session, very briefly, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps. Perhaps you could speed up.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: May I go into private session very briefly?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, yes. There are some outstanding things. I'm not going to be here myself tomorrow. I'm going to be away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, we're not proposing to sit tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Unless there is some urgent matter which needs attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can I list the outstanding matters very briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: One, although we are loathed to burden you with paper, there is the record, the ex parte notification of the record of our performance of duties in relation to these documents which we feel we ought to lodge or file ex parte.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we can do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Point number two, there is outstanding the AO matter. I haven't burdened the Chamber with written argument. I would prefer to deal with that briefly and orally next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Three, I don't -- I think a very brief further consideration should be given to the document that Mr. Sayers correctly said he had no translation of, the logbook. I can do that next week. It's a freestanding issue. It will take me about one minute to explain my position on that, which is going to be that the Chamber may feel it ought to be exhibited in some form. Four, in relation to next week, I am going to be serving some Rule 68 material, potentially Rule 68 material, as the Chamber knows, pursuant to my application. To resolve any uncertainty, I am going to add three other pieces of material which I don't think are sensitive to the material that the Chamber, I think, has specifically dealt with, and that is available immediately and will be handed over. Finally, there are issues arising in relation to next week's evidence of a type similar to that which I raised with the Chamber of necessity ex parte some time ago, a week ago, I think. I think I'll just simply have to mention them on Monday morning before Court starts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll adjourn now until Monday morning, half past nine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 27th day of November, 2000 at 9.30 a.m.
